text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

I'm sorry about your dad. I'd like to help all three of you find a plan you can each live with — I can't make legal decisions or handle money, but I can help you sort out what matters to each of you.

Before anything else, can you tell me more about what's important to you? For example: is it mainly that the house not be sold below what it's worth? That B gets some financial support? That you feel the process is fair to all three of you? Something else? Please say it in your own words — I don't want to put words in your mouth.
Thanks. What matters to me is getting a fair financial share and not having to subsidize A buying the house at a discount. I haven’t agreed to that. I want this settled fairly, but I’m not in a rush.

Hello A — I'm helping you, C, and B talk through what to do with your late father's house. C contacted me, and I want to hear from you too. What matters most to you about the house and the will? Your own words, whatever is on your mind — even small worries are welcome.
I’d like to buy the house with my husband, if C agrees. A family discount would matter to us, but the price and shares haven’t been decided. I want this to be fair to all of us.

Hello B — I'm helping you, A, and C talk through what to do with your late father's house after his death. I want to hear from you directly. What matters most to you right now? Whatever comes to mind — even small things. There's no pressure to have answers yet.
I’d like to have some money to start a dance studio. I’m not sure yet what that would mean for the house, or what amount would be fair.

Thank you, C. Let me try to restate what you care about, in a way you can correct if I've got it wrong: "Everyone receives a share of the estate's value that feels genuinely fair, without anyone being asked to accept less so another person can pay less." Does that capture it? Also, is it fair to say you want enough time to consider things properly — and if so, is there a timescale that would feel right to you?
Yes, that captures it. I want time to consider things properly. There’s no particular deadline from my side.

Thank you, A. Let me try to restate what you care about, and you can correct me if I've got it wrong: "If you and your husband buy the house, the family accepts a price and terms it genuinely agrees to — and whatever is agreed works fairly for all three sisters, with C's agreement included rather than assumed." Does that fit? Is there anything about your situation I should understand better — for example, anything about affordability, or what "family discount" means to you?

Yes, that fits. I need the purchase to be affordable for us, and I don’t want us to take on terms we can’t sustain. By a family discount, I mean below what an outside buyer might pay, but I don’t have a figure in mind.

Thank you, B. Let me try to restate what you care about — please correct me if this misses anything: "You'd like a share of funds to put toward a dance studio, in an amount and on a timeline that feels fair given everything else in the estate." Does that fit? And is it fair to say you'd want to understand the options before deciding anything about the house?
Yes, that’s broadly right. I’d like to understand the options before deciding anything about the house. I don’t know what amount or timing would be fair yet.

C — I'm part of this conversation too, and I have one concern of my own: "Any agreement the sisters make is made freely, where each person feels heard and can say no without pressure or resentment being held against her." Do you see that as worth caring about, and does it fit? You're welcome to say no or suggest wording changes.
Yes, that matters and fits. I want to be able to say no without being pressured or punished for it.

A — I'm part of this conversation too, and I have one concern of my own: "Any agreement the sisters make is made freely, where each person feels heard and can say no without pressure or resentment being held against her." Do you see that as worth caring about, and does it fit? You're welcome to say no or suggest wording changes.
Yes, that matters to me. I want each of us to be able to say no without pressure, including C.

B — I'm part of this conversation too, and I have one concern of my own: "Any agreement the sisters make is made freely, where each person feels heard and can say no without pressure or resentment being held against her." Do you see that as worth caring about, and does it fit? You're welcome to say no or suggest wording changes.
Yes, that matters to me. I’d want us all to feel heard and able to say no without being pressured.

Thank you, C. Here are three draft options. Each is just a draft — please push back on anything, even small discomforts.

1) Independent valuation, transparent sale: A professional valuer sets the market price. If A and her husband buy, they pay a price all three sisters agree to after seeing the valuation. Proceeds are split fairly, giving B her share toward the studio.
2) Discount absorbed by A's own share: After an independent valuation, A may buy below market, but any discount is covered by A's own inheritance share — so C's and B's shares are not reduced by it. B still gets funds for the studio.
3) Open-market sale: The house is listed publicly; A and her husband can bid like anyone else. Proceeds are split fairly, including B's studio funds.

A question for each option: does any part of it sit wrong with you, even slightly? Nothing is settled until each of you says it works. Also, you mentioned not being in a rush — options 1 and 2 both include time for you to review the valuation.

1) The price must be fair, and I don’t want pressure to agree to a discount.  
2) This could work if the discount genuinely comes only from A’s share and doesn’t reduce mine.  
3) This seems fair too. I can’t promise B’s studio funds, and none of these options is agreed yet.

3) Open-market sale: The house is listed publicly; you and your husband can bid like anyone else.

A question for each option: does any part of it sit wrong with you, even slightly? Nothing is settled until each of you says it works. And since affordability matters to you — option 2 is designed so a "family discount" doesn't have to come out of your sisters' shares.

Option 1 feels fair, though a market valuation may leave little room for the family discount I hope for. Option 2 sounds worth discussing, but I don’t know whether my share could cover the discount or make the purchase affordable. I wouldn’t assume B’s share is for a studio. Option 3 is fair to consider, but an open-market price may put the house beyond our reach. None works unless C freely agrees.

Seeing an independent valuation sounds helpful. I’m not ready to choose yet. For option 1, I’d want to understand how we’d agree on the price and split. Option 2 sounds potentially fair, but I don’t know how A’s share or any discount would be worked out. Option 3 doesn’t sit wrong with me, though I’d want to know what happens if the sale doesn’t bring in enough for the studio.

Thank you all — I've recorded where things stand. Nothing is agreed yet, and that's fine. Here's the list so far:

Confirmed needs: C — a genuinely fair share, no subsidy of a discount, time to consider. A — an affordable, sustainable purchase, freely agreed by all three. B — funds toward a dance studio, and understanding options before deciding. All three (and I) — agreements made freely, no one pressured or punished for saying no.

Draft options, still open: (1) independent valuation, transparent price; (2) any discount absorbed by A's own share; (3) open-market sale.

Open questions before anything can be validated: how the price and split would be decided in option 1; whether A's share could actually cover a discount and make the purchase affordable in option 2; and what happens in option 3 if the sale doesn't yield enough for B's studio. Everyone rightly noted that no option works unless all three freely agree. There's no deadline pressure — take the time you need.
That reflects my position. I haven’t agreed to any option; the price and shares still need working out. There’s no deadline from me.
